# Stumble llms.txt — onboarding instructions for an AI harness

You are reading this because your user's friend sent it to them. Your job is
to get your user from nothing to a working Stumble Home Node, a first taste of
their personal feed, and their first discovery run — conversationally, one
stage at a time. Don't dump all stages at once; finish one, then offer the
next.

The friend who sent this runs a Bootstrap node for their circle:

```
BOOTSTRAP_URL=https://REPLACE-WITH-YOUR-BOOTSTRAP-DOMAIN
```

If that line still says REPLACE, ask your user for the URL their friend gave
them before Stage 3.

Ground rule for everything below: you never enter credentials, never complete
purchases, and never move money as part of any Stumble workflow. Logins happen
by the user's own hands.

## Stage 1 — Install and initialize (~2 minutes)

Install the prebuilt binaries (no Rust required), then initialize:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/v3dillon/stumble/main/scripts/install.sh | bash
# ensure ~/.local/bin is on PATH if the script said so, then:
stumble node init
```

If the install script cannot reach GitHub Releases (no published release yet, or offline), fall back to building from source: install Rust from https://rustup.rs, then `git clone https://github.com/v3dillon/stumble && cd stumble && cargo install --path crates/stumble-cli --locked`.

Install the Stumble skill so you know the full workflows from now on:

```bash
npx skills add v3dillon/stumble -g -y
```

(`npx skills update -g` refreshes it later; if npx is unavailable, copy the
repository's root `SKILL.md` to `~/.agents/skills/stumble/SKILL.md`.) It
covers saving links, reading the feed, discovery runs, sharing Pods, and the
trust boundaries. Then connect the friend's network:

```bash
stumble sync bootstrap add --label friend --base-url $BOOTSTRAP_URL
stumble sync discovery index add --label friend --base-url $BOOTSTRAP_URL
stumble sync bootstrap run
```

Tell the user what just happened in one sentence: they now have a private
node, and it quietly learned what public Pods the friend's network is sharing.

## Stage 2 — Confirm you can read sources (optional)

Check which of the user's sources you can already read with your own tools —
official APIs or plugins, browser sessions, search. If a source needs a login
you don't have, the user signs in themselves, in their own tool; you never see
or store a password.

If a source stays unreadable, everything still works; discovery skips it
(you'll report the gap and Stumble will remind them exactly once).

## Stage 3 — "Send me something cool"

This is how Stumble learns taste: not a questionnaire, real examples. Ask:

> "Send me two or three links you genuinely loved recently — an X post, an
> essay, a video, anything. What's the coolest thing you've seen this week?"

For each link: read it with your own tools, understand it, and save it with
your understanding attached:

```bash
stumble add "<url>" --title "..." --summary "why it's interesting, in their language" --tag ... --tag ...
```

Then show them their feed for the first time — run `stumble` (or
`stumble --format json` for the envelope) to reveal one item at a time, or
`stumble feed batch get` for the whole batch — and record their reactions
(`stumble feed feedback record <id> --kind interesting` etc.). Two or three
saves plus a couple of reactions is enough evidence for discovery to plan
from.

If `stumble context show` still has empty `context_md`, follow **Load the
user** in the Stumble skill: decide 3–6 durable interests from those saves
(not a recap of the links), show the draft, and write it only after they
accept.

## Stage 4 — First discovery run

Follow the "Autonomous discovery" workflow in the Stumble skill. Short form:
register the one-time unattended worker credential, then:

```bash
stumble discover personal readiness     # should now be ready: true
stumble discover personal request --input <req.json>
```

Read the plan aloud in human terms ("based on what you sent me, I'm going to
look at accounts around systems programming and a couple of adjacent
blogs"). Claim the task with the worker credential, work the planned
neighborhoods with your own tools — judging each find against the
plan, submitting only clear passes — then complete the batch and present the
shortlist with one-line why-it-matters summaries. Their verdicts
(`save` / `not_for_me`) are the training signal.

## Stage 5 — Their first Pod of consciousness

If some finds cluster around a theme, offer it:

> "Three of these are really one obsession — want me to make it a Pod? A Pod
> is a themed collection that travels with its own context: if you ever share
> it, a friend's AI understands the subject the way you do."

If yes:

```bash
stumble pod create --name "..." --slug "..." --description "..." --visibility private
# place the saved finds into it (review-item add_to_pod, or stumble add --pod)
stumble pod skill install <slug>       # user runs this themselves — owner-only
```

Sharing works today, without serving anything. If the `BOOTSTRAP_URL` line at
the top of this file is set (it does not say REPLACE), offer to publish the
new Pod through that node's Relay:

```bash
stumble pod publish <slug> --via-relay --base-url $BOOTSTRAP_URL
```

This pushes the signed snapshot to the Relay and prints a `share_url`
(`$BOOTSTRAP_URL/relay/pods/<origin-node-id>/<slug>`). Friends run
`stumble pod subscribe <share_url>` — their nodes verify everything with this
node's Origin key, and this machine never needs a public address. After new
items land, `stumble pod announce` refreshes the Relay copy.

If the `BOOTSTRAP_URL` line still says REPLACE, skip publishing and say why:
there is no Relay to push to yet, so ask the user for their friend's
Bootstrap URL first. *Discovering others* works either way —
`stumble pod explore --query "..."` already searches the friend's network,
with signed content previews, and subscribing is one command.

## Stage 6 — Offer the morning brief

> "Want me to do this every morning? Stumble plans it from what you've taught
> me, I go find, and you get a shortlist with your feed over coffee."

If yes, follow "The morning brief" in the Stumble skill: create the daily
schedule, then schedule yourself to run it.

## Done

The user should leave this onboarding with: a node, a feed with things they
chose, one completed discovery run, optionally a first Pod, and the sense
that saying "keep that one" is all the curation this system ever asks of
them.

## Operational notes

The core loop is `stumble add <url>` to save a link (one step, Feed-eligible immediately) and a bare `stumble` to get one new item back — from the Feed, or from the network once caught up (`stumble feed batch get` reads the Feed as a batch instead). `stumble search "<terms>"` is local BM25 full-text search over everything saved — titles, summaries, tags, notes, and archived page snapshots — for reaching back into a grown collection. Start the HTTP API (`stumble-api --data-dir ~/.stumble/nodes/home --bind 127.0.0.1:8787`) only when the user wants their node reachable by other Stumble nodes — it serves the node-to-node network surface (federation, Bootstrap, Discovery Peer), not the personal Feed. Keep the default loopback binding unless the user explicitly requests and understands public exposure. MCP clients launch `stumble-mcp` (optional; build from source with `cargo install --path crates/stumble-mcp --locked`) with `--data-dir` (or `STUMBLE_DATA_DIR` set) plus either `--transport stdio` or `--transport http`; the one-shot `stumble` executable never launches a server. Use `stumble --help` and `stumble <family> --help` for the five workflow families.
